> all of the above examples (1a, 1b, 2a) should be possible because the idea behind the policy is to prevent stealing focus from the parent, not to restrict what a frame can do once it has focus.

> This tries to avoid breaking existing sites that are embedded with this policy denied so the feature can be more easily adopted, while still fulfilling the need for preventing frames from stealing focus from a parent.

I agree with this. I can only speak for my use case, which is to prevent third-party iframes (like adverts) from stealing focus from the main frame without user activation.

If the user interacts with the third party frame, then everything should proceed just as if this `focus-without-user-activation` "never existed". That is, until focus passes back up through a `focus-without-user-activation` boundary, at which point user activation is once again required for focus to go back down.

As the original author of the proposal that turned into `focus-without-user-activation` policy https://github.com/w3c/webappsec/issues/543 I can confirm the proposal here is reasonable. The use case behind the original proposal was the same as @josephrocca mentioned before me - to prevent ads from stealing focus - which should be satisfied with the changes proposed. Thanks @ffiori for your work on this and for caring about compatibility for existing systems 👏

Does anything change when (C) is same origin as (A)? (A->B->A)
Supposedly, the main frame can set focus directly on (C) because it has direct window access, but then this proposal would let (B) steal it. Who is in charge in that case, the higher level origin or the higher level frame?
Supposedly the main frame should be able to prevent stealing focus from the internal frame? But perhaps this discloses the fact that (A) and (C) are same-origin?

This might be a non-issue, but we should at least be explicit about this changing behaviour for A->B->A and whether this is OK.

> [@noamr](https://github.com/noamr) I wouldn't say anything changes policy-wise if C is same origin as A, the higher level frame is in charge. The goal and motivation of the policy is to prevent frames from unexpectedly stealing focus from the parent.
> 
> I guess in this case A could coordinate with C to focus it again, or A could choose not to host B. C could also use CSP rules to avoid being embedded by B. If we choose to restrict B from taking focus from C then this could make the policy harder to adopt because it would break those scenarios where B assumes that's possible.
> 
> I'm curious, have you seen this (parent needing to be prevented from retaking focus from its own descendant) come up in a real-world case?

No. This is purely a way to flesh out potential same-origin violations and edge cases, a some A->B->A scenarios came up in other features that had to deal with this type of policies.

https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#deferred-fetch-quota

@noamr, let me see if I'm getting the scenario you're referring to. I understand it's something along the lines of this example mentioned in the fetch spec in the link you shared:

> The following tree illustrates how quota is distributed to different nested documents in a tree:
>
> https://top.example.com, with permissions policy set to `Permissions-policy: deferred-fetch=(self "https://ok.example.com")`
> 
> - https://x.example.com: receives 8 kibibytes.
> 
>   - https://top.example.com: 0. Even though it’s same origin with the top-level traversable, it does not automatically share its quota as they are separated by a cross-origin intermediary.

Here https://x.example.com has the policy denied and is cross-origin, so it only receives the minimal quota (8kb). Then the innermost https://top.example.com receives 0kb because its frame has the policy denied, and only documents with the same origin as the top-level traversable can grant the 8kb based on the "deferred-fetch-minimal" policy (in this case https://x.example.com is not same origin as https://top.example.com so it can't grant the 8kb to the innermost frame).

This aligns with the focus policy behavior in the sense that B can't steal focus from top frame A because it's got the policy denied, and innermost frame A can't steal focus from neither B nor top level A (both parent frames) because it's got the policy denied. And this is because permissions policies depend on the frame/nesting structure, which applies to both focus-without-user-activation and deferred-fetch.

Regards this:

> This might be a non-issue, but we should at least be explicit about this changing behaviour for A->B->A and whether this is OK.

I agree this is worth being explicit about. That said, since focus-without-user-activation is not yet shipped or implemented in current browsers (nowadays any frame can programmatically move focus or steal it from a parent, except in webkit), this wouldn’t represent a behavioral change so much as defining the intended behavior up front. I'm down to add a note clarifying how the A->B->A case is treated in the specs to make it extra clear.
@ffiori to be clear this is not a specific concern or objection to this feature.

Expanding on the case where there are popups around as it came up during WHATNOT 1/29 https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12113.
 
## Proposed behavior
 
I put together a table below with the model I had in mind, assuming the **policy is enabled in the opener and denied in the popup** (if both had the policy allowed, everything would be permitted):
 
| Caller | Target | Focused | Focus call is allowed |
|-----------------|-----------------|------------------|------------------------|
| Popup           | Opener          | Opener           | No  ❌                   |
| Popup           | Popup           | Opener           | No  ❌                   |
| Popup           | Opener          | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
| Popup           | Popup           | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Opener          | Opener           | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Popup           | Opener           | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Opener          | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Popup           | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
 
Under this model, the only forbidden cases are when the popup calls `focus()` on anything while the opener is currently focused, because that represents the popup trying to move focus away from the opener without permission. Conceptually this matches the same behavior as with nested browsing contexts: the child cannot take focus from the parent without permission.
 
## Spec behavior
 
I don't see much in the spec about popups and focus (please point me to where that is in case I'm missing something). So I understand this would behave the same as iframes following the [allow focus steps](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#allow-focus-steps): if the popup has the policy disabled, all focus **calls with the popup as target would be forbidden** (No delegation possible), while all others where the opener is the target would be allowed (notice this would allow the popup to call `window.opener.focus()`)
 
| Caller | Target | Focused | Focus call is allowed |
|-----------------|-----------------|------------------|------------------------|
| Popup           | Opener          | Opener           | Yes ✅                   |
| Popup           | Popup           | Opener           | No  ❌                   |
| Popup           | Opener          | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
| Popup           | Popup           | Popup            | No  ❌                   |
| Opener          | Opener          | Opener           | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Popup           | Opener           | No  ❌                   |
| Opener          | Opener          | Popup            | Yes ✅                   |
| Opener          | Popup           | Popup            | No  ❌                   |
 
## Current behavior in browsers
 
I did some testing locally and it seems like the current behavior (chromium/Firefox/Safari) is that the popup can't move focus to the opener even if it's focused, and vice-versa the opener can't focus on the popup if the focus is on the opener. Seems like the focused window always wins and you can't programmatically move focus between them (unless the user does it).
 
I rewrite the same table as before with the currently implemented behavior, notice that the only allowed cases are when **target document === focused document**:
 
| Caller | Target | Focused | Focus call is allowed |
|-----------------|-----------------|------------------|------------------------|
| Popup           | Opener          | Opener           | Yes ✅|
| Popup           | Popup           | Opener           | No  ❌                  |
| Popup           | Opener          | Popup            | No  ❌                  |
| Popup           | Popup           | Popup            | Yes ✅                  |
| Opener          | Opener          | Opener           | Yes ✅                  |
| Opener          | Popup           | Opener           | No  ❌                  |
| Opener          | Opener          | Popup            | No  ❌                  |
| Opener          | Popup           | Popup            | Yes ✅                  |
